summary: Sekhmet Sync harmonizes 24 years of NASA FIRMS fire detections from MODIS and VIIRS into one consistent California record. The two sensors see the same fires differently — MODIS at 1 km, VIIRS at 375 m, with different overpass times and detection limits — so adding their counts double-counts fires and creates false jumps when satellites change. We solve this by counting cell-days: one 1-km square burning for one day, counted once, translated into MODIS-equivalent numbers with calibration factors fitted on 2012–2019 overlap data. The result is a single daily series covering 8,827 days from 2000 to 2024, with 94,125 burning cell-days in 2020–2024. At annual totals it matches MODIS within 2% in 2022–2024. Our web app lets anyone pick a California region and timeframe, explore the burning calendar, compare against the historical median, and download the data. A consistent record like this is essential for spotting real wildfire trends, and for the fire planning that depends on them, instead of mistaking sensor changes for changes on the ground.
details:
What it does and how it works

We built Sekhmet Sync because MODIS and VIIRS don't agree with each other. They watch the same fires in California, but MODIS sees them at 1 km and VIIRS at 375 m, they pass over at different times, and they don't pick up the same small fires. So if you just add their numbers together, you count the same fire twice, and every time a new satellite shows up your chart jumps for no real reason.

We tried the obvious stuff first. Adding pixels. Scaling by fire power. Clustering. Dividing by how many satellites were up. Each one fixed one jump and left another one standing.

So we stopped trying to make the pixels match and changed what we count. One cell-day: one 1-km square, burning for one day, counted once. Every day gets one number, never two. MODIS gives us the real number through 2019, and after that we translate VIIRS into MODIS numbers, using two calibration numbers we fit from the years where both satellites were watching — 1.0602 for S-NPP, 1.1183 for NOAA-20. That gives us one daily series, 8,827 days from 2000 to 2024, with 94,125 burning cell-days in 2020–2024.

The app is the part people actually touch. Pick a part of California and a timeframe, look at the burning calendar, compare a year to the usual median, download the data as a CSV. Every row tells you where the number came from.

Why it matters

If the record keeps jumping every time a satellite changes, you can't tell what's actually burning more and what's just a sensor change. A clean record means fire agencies, researchers, and anyone else can compare this year to the past on the same scale, spot a bad year early, and plan around real trends. And because the data and code are public and every number traces back to its source, anyone can check our work instead of taking our word for it.

Tools we used

Python, with pandas, NumPy, and Plotly. The app is Streamlit, hosted on Streamlit Cloud, and the code lives on GitHub. Bulk history came from the NASA FIRMS Archive — the API was only for recent data in the Situational Awareness tab. AI coding tools helped us write code — Antigravity, Kiro, Codex — but we directed them, reviewed everything, and checked the numbers ourselves. The method and the decisions were ours. No special hardware, just a PC.

What makes it creative

The cell-day. Instead of forcing two different sensors to agree pixel by pixel, we made them agree on something physical — a square kilometre burning for a day — and then proved the translation works. The twin check matches MODIS in 8 out of 8 years from 2012 to 2019, and at annual totals we're within 2% of MODIS in 2022–2024. We also show where it's weakest. In 2020 we over-predict by 16%, and we say that openly instead of hiding it.

What we kept in mind

Three things, really. Don't double-count. Keep it simple enough that someone who isn't a remote sensing person can use it. And don't hide the limits — if a number is shaky, the user should be able to see that, not find out later.
